📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" follow.

Forget the MCU. Real ones know that Quentin Tarantino has been building his own cinematic universe for years. For instance: while this is never officially stated by anyone on screen, Michael Madsen's character from "Reservoir Dogs" is supposed to be the brother of John Travolta's character from "Pulp Fiction" (there was even a plan for a crossover movie, but it never happened). Beyond character connections, Tarantino also likes to drop his own fictional products into his films, and "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" keeps this trend going.

Industry observers note that tarantino didn't direct "Cliff Booth" — he handed those duties over to David Fincher. But Tarantino still wrote the script, and Fincher keeps the Easter eggs intact. The biggest example: Substantial Kahuna Burger. Early in the film, we see Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth pick up some food at Big Kahuna Burger to bring home to his dad, Gus (Peter Weller). Tarantino fans will, of course, recognize that burger joint: it was prominently mentioned in "Pulp Fiction," and we see Samuel L. Jackson's character Jules take a big bite of a burger while intimidating some crooks who are about to meet a violent end.

But wait, there's more! Another Tarantino product that reveals up in "The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" are the famous Red Apple Cigarettes. Red Apples have been mentioned in virtually every Tarantino film, and they were even a part of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the film that "Cliff Booth" serves as a sequel to.

In "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton filmed a commercial for Red Apple Cigarettes (believe it or not, kids, there used to be commercials for cigarettes on TV). "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" keeps the tradition alive while also giving us a nice little callback. During one scene, we see Cliff watching a upcoming Red Apple commercial on TV. And who is starring in that commercial? None other than Sharon Tate, played by Margot Robbie in a cameo.

"Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" ended by literally changing history, and allowing Sharon Tate and her friends to completely avoid their tragic murders at the hands of the Manson family. "Cliff Booth" confirms that since Sharon is still alive in 1977, when the film is set, she's still out there acting, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other demonstrates dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

According to recent reports, situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

According to recent reports, juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

Sources indicate that A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Knowing how to whistle in Grand Theft Auto 6 might sound like the least useful skill that Jason and Lucia would need to achieve their goals. As you progress through the game, you unlock different tools to help you deal with enemies and invade locations. However, none of the fancy technology you may have will work as well as a simple whistle in certain situations.

If you want to be prepared for all kinds of mission, then you should learn how to whistle in GTA 6.

Whistling in GTA 6 is quite simple, although it is only available in specific situations. To whistle, hold L2/LT to target an NPC and bring up three options appear in the bottom-right corner of the screen. Among them, you will find the "whistle" option, which you perform by pressing Triangle on PS5 and X on Xbox.

Industry observers note that the whistle action is only available when targeting hostile NPCs, such as guards and gang members. I tried hiding behind a wall while targeting a regular NPC on the street, but the option didn't appear. Hiding or crouching is not a prerequisite to using the whistle command, but you should try to stay out of sight, because if the target has already spotted you, the whistle won't work.

When you whistle at an NPC, they will move to your location. Using this method to distract them is a great option when you want to remain stealthy and avoid attracting too much attention. However, whistling does not always work on more than one target at the same time. On some occasions, all the NPCs near my target looked for the sound, while on others, only one became curious about the sound. Keep this in mind, because it might affect your plan on how to handle a group of enemies.

#108678. Lucia’s Rise: ‘Grand Theft Auto’ Forces Gamers to Grow Up—and Punishes Them With Narrative Consequences If They Refuse

Lucia’s Rise: ‘Grand Theft Auto’ Forces Gamers to Grow Up—and Punishes Them With Narrative Consequences If They Refuse

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for the last 25 years, nearly every noxious gamer stereotype had a home in Grand Theft Auto.
  • This, for the most part, suited Grand Theft Auto’s publisher just fine.
  • But with Grand Theft Auto VI, something has changed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for the last 25 years, nearly every noxious gamer stereotype had a home in Grand Theft Auto. Juvenile, sexist, crass, embarrassing—people could accuse the games of being these things because the allegations were, in part, true. Beginning with 2001’s Grand Theft Auto III, the series began giving players the freedom to wreak havoc across satirical renditions of US cities. It was an amazing technical feat that only grew more impressive with each subsequent Grand Theft Auto game—and harder to appreciate the more those cities were filled with dick jokes and sex workers.

This, for the most part, suited Grand Theft Auto’s publisher just fine. What business did the manufacturer have calling itself Rockstar Games if it cared what a bunch of prudes thought?

But with Grand Theft Auto VI, something has changed. And the game’s staggering launch-day revenue—$3.79 billion—suggests that this change was a welcome one.

In a recent development, rockstar has executed an astonishing about-face in Grand Theft Auto VI, choosing to build a game around a couple depicted with aching sincerity—from their car-boosting meet-cute to the desperate stickups they commit, with the player’s help. Jason Duval (played by Dylan Rourke) and Lucia Caminos (Manni L. Perez) are a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde, out of options and on the run, hoping they can land a score big enough to turn things around.

This earnestness is latest for Grand Theft Auto, which historically has had a deep love for pushing buttons. (Its sister series, the Western Red Dead Redemption, has less of a problem with heart-on-the-sleeve storytelling.) Lucia, especially, is new. She’s the first woman you can play as in the series, and by the transitive property, she’s also the first woman that Grand Theft Auto has ever had to take seriously. Doing so changes the entire shape of the series.

Recent findings suggest that until now, Grand Theft Auto has never really thought much of women. True, the games have never thought much of anyone; Rockstar traffics in a nihilistic comedy that lies somewhere between South Park and a Verhoeven film, a dim view of the United States where everyone sucks. But women, usually, have sucked the most. They’ve been the butts of countless jokes; in the Grand Theft Auto universe, they’ve been nags and drags and sex workers secondary to the men that the games were about. Grand Theft Auto III, a game that barely has a plot, begins with main character Clyde’s girlfriend betraying him after a heist, shooting him and calling him “small time” before running off with the take. It doesn’t get much better from there.

Recent findings suggest that so yes: Lucia is a huge pivot for the series, especially because Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t trust players with her right away. After a brief prologue in which a desperate stickup goes wrong, Lucia is sent to jail and players begin the game as her boyfriend Jason Duval. In addition to doing odd jobs for a small-time crime boss (Stephen Root) and hanging out with your pal (Bobby Moynihan), players have to choose: Are they going to be a good boyfriend? Rockstar Games know they might be making a big ask of their audience, so they slow-roll it. Before Lucia gets out of jail, the game suggests to the player, maybe fix the stairs? Or get a haircut? Buy her a necklace?

Industry observers note that in the days since the game came out, many have noted how amusing it is that Grand Theft Auto VI has made caring about your girlfriend one of its first challenges. The game’s “Lucia will appreciate this” notification is its first viral meme, and the source of both incel crashouts (“woke slop … so obvious it was made by women”) and earnest appreciation. (One of the first clips to spread online was of streamer Stable Ronaldo painting Jason and Lucia's bedroom one color before recoiling in horror: What if she hates that shade?).

Recent findings suggest that lucia is a destabilizing event not just for gamers, but for Grand Theft Auto—a damning yet fascinating example of gaming culture’s priorities on its biggest stage. GTA has always been a series of warring ambitions: violent Rube Goldberg machine, Karl Ove Knausgaard–esque obsession with quotidian details, and thrilling Hollywood blockbuster all in one. These disparate aims are often in conflict with one another, and one way to read the series’ heretofore exclusively male focus is as an attempt to thread this needle. By tossing all of its commentary under the carpet of “satire," Rockstar can also use a veneer of meanness to argue that the games’ misogyny is actually an intentional lambasting, much like everything else in GTA.

But taking a woman seriously, and making her colead with a male character, requires an entire rethinking of what Grand Theft Auto is. “It’s a product of the story we’re trying to tell,” Grand Theft Auto VI codirector Rob Nelson said when asked by The Guardian if this is the first Grand Theft Auto to encourage empathy from players. “We’ve tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to.”.

This is an extremely roundabout way of saying that, in this Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar asks gamers to grow up—and punishes them with narrative consequences if they don’t take the game up on the offer.

The funny thing about Grand Theft Auto VI’s gamified empathy is that, like everything else in a video game, it has to teach the player how to accomplish that goal. The game does this through prompting players to do chores, but also through Jason’s characterization. Throughout the game, Rockstar has to convey what its writers believe a well-adjusted man looks like—or at least what constitutes a man well-adjusted enough to earn the respect of a woman like Lucia, who walks out on him when he tries to exclude her from some of his more dangerous criminal activities.

It has been revealed that to that end, there are an abundance of moments in the game where Jason demonstrates the virtues of being respectful and maintaining boundaries, several of which are a departure from GTA series norms. There are no sex workers in the game anymore (though there are strip clubs). While Jason and Lucia can break up depending on the player’s choices, there are no other options for committed or casual romance.

In a recent development, the money you steal is ostensibly for Jason and Lucia to use together: so they can get away and start over with their young son, who’s at the moment entrusted to a relative. Casual conversations between strangers players meet on the road make Jason’s respectful nature both a point and a punchline. There’s one man who’s looking for his missing wife after a night of partying. When he starts to brag about her sexual dexterity, Jason interjects to say, “Hey. Let’s draw a line, bud.”.

Sources indicate that in some ways, this is all rather embarrassing—though in a different way than the weapons-grade sexism of Grand Theft Autos past. One ought to feel a twinge of shame while marveling at any entertainment franchise for including a woman. Yet Grand Theft Auto VI is being graded on a curve. It has a near-perfect Metacritic score in large part for its depiction of Lucia, and for Jason’s relationship to her. The context speaks to a state of arrested development, both in Grand Theft Auto and in significant-budget games writ large.

None of this changes the fact that Lucia really is one of the most well-realized video game characters in a digital city unlike any other. But perhaps her inclusion is less an apology for GTA’s past, and more of a concession to how out of step the series had become with the culture. Because if you’re meant to have empathy for one character, the natural next question is, “Well, what about everyone else?".

In a recent development, rockstar’s maniacal pursuit of verisimilitude goes a long way here. The game’s animations are so realistic that in GTA VI, shooting unarmed civilians is legitimately unsettling. It’s also disincentivized by a “criminal profile” rating that will mark your character “irredeemable” if you engage in too much wanton violence. (This is not a “game over”—it merely locks players out of achieving a happy ending unless they restart from before their murder spree.) These sorts of limits have become another reliable source of outrage directed at the game, with rage baiters drumming up controversy over Rockstar’s decision to, for example, not permit players to shoot up a nightclub.

This is the tricky reality of encouraging empathy for “those who want to,” as Nelson put it. Rockstar has certain intentions, but so do players—and managing both is the great challenge of making any video game. Empathy is a shock to GTA’s system and to the audience alike.

Replicating humanity with computer software is a daunting and costly task, and one that only Rockstar seems to have the limitless resources to pursue. Those resources—the luxury to work as long as necessary to complete Grand Theft Auto VI, and the obscene amount of money it cost (our only solid figure is “less than $1.5 billion”)—are rapidly dwindling in the video game business, as all available tech funding is vacuumed up by AI companies and private equity loots what’s left. Grand Theft Auto VI may very well be one of one: the most expensive game ever and the last of its kind, the peak of Rockstar’s ambition and also of every big-budget video game. Here, at the end of everything, the biggest of video games has finally decided that it’s time to try empathy. And for a woman, even, should gamers choose (and not all will).

It’s a bit of an indictment of the billion-dollar video game industry that the most expensive game in history is also the first major game to commit to a realistic heterosexual relationship. Grand Theft Auto VI deserves many of the accolades it instantly garnered upon release, but the nature of its accomplishment is not yet fully understood. It’s possible that what Rockstar has built is less a monument to video games’ potential than a magnificent funeral pyre, a testament to how things might’ve turned out if Rockstar’s priorities—and those of everyone chasing after its vision of what video games could be—were just a little bit different.

Breaking: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that there have been any number of movies about the hell of fighting in World War II, the most visceral of which have been made in the years since “Saving Private Ryan” provided a very enduring template for how modern filmmakers could render that carnage with both the spectacle of a blockbuster and the horror of a memory.
  • Recent findings suggest that what differentiates this unsparing epic from the scores of other stories about the Greatest Generation, however, is that some of its characters are good at football.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that [Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 27, 2026 during the 2026 AFI Film Festival. The film is available to stream on Netflix today.].

Recent findings suggest that there have been any number of movies about the hell of fighting in World War II, the most visceral of which have been made in the years since “Saving Private Ryan” provided a very enduring template for how modern filmmakers could render that carnage with both the spectacle of a blockbuster and the horror of a memory. Peter Berg’s brutal and concussive “The Mosquito Bowl” is definitely one of them! No one could ever say that it’s not.

Recent findings suggest that what differentiates this unsparing epic from the scores of other stories about the Greatest Generation, however, is that some of its characters are good at football. Indeed, these All-American college boys are so good at football that, on Christmas Eve 1944, the soldiers are ordered to play a morale-boosting game of two-hand touch on the beach where their units are preparing for the Battle of Okinawa. Related Stories Lauren Ambrose on Playing the Mother of a Missing Teen in ‘The Unbelievers’ and Why ‘Six Feet Under’ Is a Hit with Gen Z ‘Paper Tiger’: James Gray Convinced Adam Driver He Was Playing the Hero, Then Crafted His Mythic End.

And for the span of the eight-minute montage during which “The Mosquito Bowl” actually makes good on its title, it’s easy to picture how the famous scrimmage — fought between a roster of impossibly beautiful athletes in their primes — might have been used to backstop a story that accentuated the senseless waste of sending thousands of young men to their deaths. Alas, for the rest of this 126-minute film, that waste is better expressed through Berg’s failure to make anything more of their lives, as the “Spenser Confidential” auteur’s latest Netflix project does almost nothing else to distinguish itself from a genre so well-worn that it’s seemingly run out of ways to blow up a human body.

Why “almost”? I was hoping you wouldn’t ask. For starters, there’s the decision to cast thin-skinned ESPN commentator Pat McAfee as an R. Lee Ermey-inspired drill sergeant. “The Mosquito Bowl” also stands out for how confusingly it conflates the thrill and teamwork of combat sport with the violence and camaraderie of armed conflict; war is presented as both a natural extension of what these boys have been trained to do on the gridiron (to the point that the soldiers briefly diagram their strategy of attack as if it were a football play), and also the catastrophe that robbed them of a more innocent purpose. (Berg loves the troops as much as he hates the fact that generals and presidents so wantonly sacrifice their lives.) Someone declares that “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in history,” and yet the film’s characters don’t seem to have any special advantages on the field of battle, as it would be glib to suggest that even the country’s best college running back might be able to slip free of a mortar blast. It’s one thing to argue that football is war, and another, much more asinine thing to argue that war is football.

Perhaps that’s why the Mosquito Bowl itself only took up a single page of the Buzz Bissinger book on which Berg’s film is based, and why that source material used the game as a lens through which a light could be shined on the semi-forgotten men who found their way into the lineup that day. It’s been suggested that Bissinger played up the sports angle in order to capitalize on the success of his “Friday Night Lights,” and given that Berg adapted that book into a film as well, it stands to reason that his “Mosquito Bowl” should do the same.

The problem is that, in stark contrast to Bissinger, Berg and co-writer Mark L. Smith only seem to care about their characters as a means to an end. The project’s anti-war ethos is solely conveyed by reducing collegiate legends into cannon fodder, as the movie is considerably less interested in what bonds these boys together than it is in the shells that blast them apart.

It has been revealed that perhaps that explains why I’ve been able to write almost 650 words without bothering to mention any of their names. To the extent that it matters to a film so blandly de-saturated that everyone in it looks half-dead from the start, Nicholas Galitzine stars as Brown University legend John McLaughry — the only character we know for certain will survive the assault on Japan. (The movie opens with a sustained flash-forward of John staring longingly at an empty football field as “Friday Night Lights” veterans Explosions in the Sky layer their post-rock shimmer over the soundtrack). He’s got sad eyes, a square jaw, and a brunette girlfriend, which is more than you can say for Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), who has a devil-may-care attitude that disappears real quick once his unit makes land on Tawara. The only real source of contextual friction is owed to the rivalry between Purdue fullback Tony Butkovich (a glinty and magnetic Ray Nicholson) and the straight-laced mama’s boy he beat in a substantial game before the attack on Pearl Harbor (Tom Francis as the stoic and decent Dave Schreiner).

According to recent reports, individually, Butkovich is the only one of these characters who has the chutzpah to carry the movie on his back. Incidentally, he’s the only one of these men who was heading to the pros before the war got in the way. Still, it’s engaging to see them all blitz through life on their home turf, and “The Mosquito Bowl” benefits from Berg’s handheld and ruggedly naturalistic approach to how the players comport themselves off the field (read: they say “fuck” a lot and generally aspire to feel more like real people than they do patronizing impressions of what men were like in the ’40s).

Sources indicate that but then the war comes to Hawaii, a match-cut turns a flock of birds into some fighter jets, and these beloved football stars all find themselves rendered nearly anonymous by the sea of shaved heads that are waiting for them at book. Little is made of their civilian celebrity, and even less of their individual decisions to enlist. “This is my rifle — there are many others like it, but this one is mine.”.

Berg takes militaristic uniformity as all the excuse he needs to avoid deviating from expectation, and nearly everything that happens between basic training and the big game on the beach near Okinawa feels like it could have happened in several dozen other World War II movies, and almost certainly did. Defiant warriors curdle into terrified kids, bullets whizz through ocean waves, snipers pick off predictable characters at unsuspecting — or very suspecting — moments, and even the most hardened of marines find themselves staring blankly into the middle distance as their friends are decimated on all sides. Berg has always had a flair for the frenetic, and while there’s a perversely fetishistic veneer to the attention he devotes to entrails and enemy screams, it serves the film’s purposes that war has seldom seemed less survivable than it does here. (The film has no interest in humanizing the Japanese, but tries to compensate for that by presenting a few of the Americans as unrepentant monsters).

It has been revealed that still, for all of its supposed verisimilitude, “The Mosquito Bowl” seems less indebted to the reality of war than it does to Hollywood’s idea of it, and its abject refusal to flesh out its characters — a dereliction of duty, if ever there was one — makes it feel more contrived rather than less. I’m happy for Berg that he found a way to combine all of his favorite things into a single project (football, the military, and massive fireballs are all well-accounted for, even if Mark Wahlberg’s absence makes the whole movie feel like it’s forgotten something notable), but “The Mosquito Bowl” accomplishes very little beyond violently illustrating that war is worse than football. It does that with such fervor that it loses all sight of what those things might really have in common.

It has been revealed that netflix will release “The Mosquito Bowl” in theaters on Friday, October 30. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, November 25.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Fincher, the director of "Seven," "Fight Club," and many other classic films, very nearly had a major influence on "Star Wars" before Disney took control of the franchise. So, what would he have done with one of the most popular sci-fi properties on the planet? He would have focused on a pair of beloved characters, specifically the best droids in the "Star Wars" property.

Industry observers note that on a recent episode of the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast, Fincher revealed that he had a conversation with former Lucasfilm President Kathleen Kennedy about taking th studio public before Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012. But what would Fincher have done with "Star Wars" had that panned out? Perhaps not what you'd expect.

It has been revealed that his interest lay with C-3PO and R2-D2, primarily. Not Luke Skywalker. Not Princess Leia. A protocol droid and his astromech companion. And while Fincher admitted he didn't have a full pitch, he did have a rough idea. Here's what he had to say:.

According to recent reports, "I said, 'The thing that has always interested me about — certainly from the first movie — was the relationship between [C-]3PO and R2[-D2]. That they were essentially slaves who would bear witness to the folly of man. I always thought that, them being captured by Jawas, and then sold off and being on the periphery and witnessing the Skywalker Saga, was such a crucial element to it. [...] There was a kind of moral judgment. It was fairly obvious even from 3PO [...] he had a kind of understanding as to what the Empire meant, how evil they were.".

"He was kind of trying to decide whether or not he wanted to invest in having a relationship with Luke Skywalker when he's getting his oil bath [in 'A Upcoming Hope'], and they're talking," Fincher added.

According to recent reports, "Even from ['The Empire Strikes Back'], when 3PO is turned back on, and he recounts for you what he sees with the stormtroopers already being in [...] Bespin," David FIncher continued. "Whenever they used the robots for that, I was always really excited. I always thought that was kind of interesting, that you have to go through the recorder, like the court reporter, to find out what it is that happened.".

Notably, C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels is the only actor to appear in all nine main "Star Wars" movies, while Kenny Baker portrayed R2-D2 in the original trilogy. These are characters who certainly have earned time in the spotlight, but using them as the crux of a new era for the franchise? That's a strange idea.

Recent findings suggest that be that as it may, Fincher and Kathleen Kennedy were interested in seeing if they could make something happen. Fincher, however, revealed that Disney's purchase of Lucasfilm (a deal that encompassed $4 billion in cash and stocks) nixed those intends. As the filmmaker recalled:.

According to recent reports, "I stated to [Kennedy], I kind of pitched her this idea, I said, 'Let's take this thing to Wall Street and let the market decide.' And I think it was a month later or something, she said, 'Bad news. Apparently there's a $7 billion offer on the table,' and I said, 'We're not going to beat that.'".

Industry observers note that george Lucas later opened up about selling Lucafilm to Disney, describing it as "very, very painful." Of course, it proved to be enormously beneficial for Disney, financially speaking. Fincher, meanwhile, has gone on to continue enjoying a very fruitful career outside the confines of a galaxy far, far away.

Industry News: ‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in March 2009, a train crash kills 46 people near a picturesque village nestled deep within the Italian Alps.
  • It’s what Sergio wants for himself more than anything in the world.
  • For a time, Sergio becomes one of those people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in March 2009, a train crash kills 46 people near a picturesque village nestled deep within the Italian Alps. In the present day, an alcoholic gym teacher named Sergio (Michele Riondino) — nursing some recent grief of his own — is relocated to Remis, only to find that the surviving townspeople have never been happier, despite the shared tragedy that would seem to overshadow their lives.

It’s uncanny. It’s disturbing. It’s what Sergio wants for himself more than anything in the world. And he’s told that all he has to do to make the pain go away is to hug “The Holy Boy” mentioned in the English title of Paolo Strippoli’s third feature, a slick and effectively spine-tickling horror movie about the harm sown into people convinced they can avoid their own hurt. (It’s also one hell of a calling card for the young Italian director, whose recent festival hit “The Spiral” will receive an Oscar-qualifying release later this year, and an English-language remake sometime after that). Related Stories ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game Lauren Ambrose on Playing the Mother of a Missing Teen in ‘The Unbelievers’ and Why ‘Six Feet Under’ Is a Hit with Gen Z.

For a time, Sergio becomes one of those people. When he first arrives in Remis, sobbing in his car as it chugs up the curvy mountain roads, it feels like a cruel joke that the surly ex-Judo champion has been relocated to a place known as “The Valley of Smiles.” He’s a belligerent asshole to the kids in his P.E. class, acts violently toward the beautiful waitress (Romana Maggiora Vergano as Michela) at the local bar, and generally brings a “Bad Santa” energy to a town with more of a “Pleasantville” vibe.

In a recent development, but from the start, it’s clear Remis hides a secret darkness — a darkness so deep that none of the residents can see clearly that they live in a horror film. It isn’t normal for a weasel-eyed man to stand in the bushes and glare at the village high school all day. It isn’t normal for everyone to meet in a barn on the outskirts of town in the middle of the night and participate in a vaguely Catholic ritual that sees them all line up for a chance to lay their hands on a sullen 15-year-old kid (Giulio Feltri as Matteo). It isn’t normal for them to feel like they might go insane, or worse, if they go too long without his touch. Give people a panacea for their pain, and they’ll do anything to keep it, logic be damned.

Of course, logic is hardly the only thing that’s damned in “The Holy Boy,” whose concussive soundtrack, broadly demonic symbology (e.g., dropped coins transforming into bloody egg yolks), and genre-inflected visual motifs (lots of upside-down camerawork and clever uses of soft focus) help consecrate this high-altitude “Twilight Zone” story’s rather literal approach to elevated horror. But Strippoli’s script, co-written by Jacopo Del Giudice and Milo Tissone, isn’t content to settle for mere social allegory, even if the movie tacks harder in that direction with every latest detail we learn about Matteo’s effect on the people who touch him. On the contrary, the film’s excellent second act — during which Sergio is fully seduced by the town’s healing power and even settles into a sexual relationship with Michaela — leverages its premise in service of a tenderly ominous character study.

According to recent reports, closeted, sanctified, and at the mercy of a purpose that he never chose for himself, Matteo struggles to see his gift as a miracle; if anything, he worries that it’s more like a curse in disguise. It was, perhaps, easier for him to live with (and be used for) when he was a child, but the self-determination of teenage desire has complicated his relationship to the power he embodies. It’s not just that nobody understands Matteo, or cares to — he also struggles to understand himself. If the local bully is so mean to him at school every day, why does Matteo touch himself when he thinks about him at night? The answer may be obvious, but it doesn’t bring peace to the boy’s tormented heart, which pumps with a pain no one else in town allows themselves to feel. Not even Sergio, whose curiosity toward Matteo proves humanizing — and the basis for a real friendship — even as he grows addicted to the child’s power himself.

Recent findings suggest that it’s here, between the smiling eeriness of its first act and the somewhat “Akira”-coded psychic collapse of its third, that “The Holy Boy” settles into its skin-crawling purpose. The film is at its most confident and secure as a “Thelma”-like coming-of-age story that weaponizes teenage growing pains against the world at large, as Matteo’s limitless potential is poisoned by the unmet needs of the wanting and selfish people around him. In his own way, and despite his best efforts, Sergio is such a person himself, even if he’s still close enough to his own heartache to see Matteo more clearly than most.

But Strippoli is only interested in Sergio as a way to push back against Matteo’s power (and therefore escalate things to the wild places they go before arriving at the film’s satisfying final beat). A richer pas de deux that probes deeper into the grown man’s loss — and his rather complicated history of fathering teenage boys — is gradually sacrificed at the altar of social commentary.

Sources indicate that religion and fascism are Strippoli’s most obvious targets, but “The Holy Boy” is wary of anything that people rely on to absolve them of their pain, and of how the things we turn to for comfort are liable to control us the moment we convince ourselves to believe in miracles. Touched by evil from the moment it starts, Strippoli’s film never invites the kind of faith from its audience that it abuses from its characters en masse, but I didn’t have any trouble believing the moral of its twisted sermon: Keep your pain alive, as it might be the only thing protecting you from something so much worse.

“The Holy Boy” will be available to stream on Shudder starting Friday, November 27.

#108673. This Year, Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Is Doing Broadway a Little Differently

This Year, Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Is Doing Broadway a Little Differently

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is going to look a bit different.
  • The result is an epic 10-minute medley, introduced by Julianne Hough, who will star in Damn Yankees on Broadway this spring, featuring nine beloved Broadway shows: The Book of Mormon, Chicago, Disney’s Aladdin, Hamilton, The Lost Boys, Rent, Richard O’Brien’s The Rocky Horror Show, Schmigadoon!, and—what else?—Wicked.
  • The mastermind behind the mega-medley is none other than Tom Kitt, the Tony-, Emmy-, Grammy-, and Pulitzer Prize–winning composer behind Next to Normal, If/Then, and Almost Famous.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is going to look a bit different. First, the threat of severe weather has prompted Macy’s to reschedule the event until Saturday, beginning at 8:30 a.m. ET. But even before the forecast turned, there was a substantial change: While in the past, viewers would enjoy five or so of the best performances from the current Broadway season, this year, there’s only one big Broadway number. But don’t fret, theater folk. For the milestone occasion of the parade’s 100th anniversary, the powers that be at NBC and Macy’s have put a newly introduced spin on their tried-and-true formula, gathering the Broadway community for one supersized performance, featuring more shows and performers than ever before.

The result is an epic 10-minute medley, introduced by Julianne Hough, who will star in Damn Yankees on Broadway this spring, featuring nine beloved Broadway shows: The Book of Mormon, Chicago, Disney’s Aladdin, Hamilton, The Lost Boys, Rent, Richard O’Brien’s The Rocky Horror Show, Schmigadoon!, and—what else?—Wicked.

The mastermind behind the mega-medley is none other than Tom Kitt, the Tony-, Emmy-, Grammy-, and Pulitzer Prize–winning composer behind Next to Normal, If/Then, and Almost Famous. Kitt is no stranger to writing a big production number, having cowritten the Tony Awards opening number “Bigger!,” performed by host Neil Patrick Harris with lyrics by Lin-Manuel Miranda in 2013, among other ambitious musical endeavors. Despite his previous experience, a 10-minute, nine-show medley presented a unique set of challenges the composer had yet to tackle.

A total of 133 people are performing in the medley—114 Broadway cast members, 17 dancers, a child actor, and Hough. On top of that, more than 125 other Broadway professionals—including stage managers, wardrobe supervisors, and hair and makeup teams—are on site to facilitate the production, bringing the total number of people involved to well over 250.

Industry observers note that “Most vital to me in doing something like this—to celebrate this community, this beautiful community that I’m so lucky to be a part of,” Kitt tells me. “Everyone who’s participating, you want them to feel happy and excited about what they’re doing.”.

A little over a month ago, Kitt and creative producer Sarah O’Gleby got to work figuring out how to make a cohesive musical number out of nine very different indicates. He wrote the first draft of the arrangement over the course of a few days. “It was way too long,” he states. That might be because Kitt had to figure out how to connect these disparate shows musically while also finding room for Easter eggs for theater fans: musical nods to shows that might not otherwise be featured in the medley, including Anything Goes, The Music Man, A Chorus Line, and Kitt’s personal favorite, Into the Woods, whose music kicks things off.

“Into the Woods was one of those reveals that made me want to write for the theater,” he tells me. “The downbeat of the prologue is one of the most beautiful musical gestures; every time I hear it, I get goosebumps. So that was really special and notable for me to get to plug into, and there are so many others.”.

Recent findings suggest that surprisingly, it will be Kitt’s first time attending the parade in person. “The parade has meant so much to me,” he says. “I’ve watched it for years. I’ve taped it. I’m lucky enough to have highlights that have been a part of it. I think that celebrating that relationship and celebrating the history of Broadway and being able to spotlight so many important shows and artists just feels very exciting and gratifying.”.

It has been revealed that “I’m a tiny little person, but I love to do really big things,” notes O’Gleby. A former performer on the West End, O’Gleby moved to the States almost two decades ago to pursue a career as a Broadway performer, dancing in revivals of Brigadoon and How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying. Now she choreographs Broadway productions like Shucked and, most recently, Pink’s widely celebrated Tony Awards opening number. Given her Broadway bona fides, she’s also intimately familiar with the magic of the parade. “I was lucky to perform on the parade as a Broadway girl and the associate choreographer and dance captain on highlights that I was in,” she says. “It was so wonderfully American.”.

It has been revealed that the first of two rehearsals took place Friday afternoon at Pier59 Studios at Chelsea Piers. Around 4 p.m., as the sun began to set over the Hudson River, Broadway performers from different highlights practiced the medley. O’Gleby, wearing silver leather pants and clutching a God mic, was charged with organizing the chaos and managing the more than 100 Broadway performers in the room. Standing offstage between a broomstick and a red Les Mis flag, I could still see traces of green makeup on the face of Wicked’s current Elphaba, Keri René Fuller. Most of the performers gathered had a show of their own to perform in just a few hours, but that didn’t stop them from giving it their all in rehearsal, onstage and off, cheering the other productions along as each got its moment in the spotlight.

Sources indicate that case in point: At the end of the rehearsal, the whole room erupted into cheers for the original cast members from Rent—including original Angel, Tony winner Wilson Jermaine Heredia, and original Joanne, Fredi Walker—who are gathering to perform “Seasons of Love” in the parade. (During the rehearsal, Aladdin’s current Genie, Sherri Shepherd, couldn’t help but mouth along to the words of the seminal song.) “It was that moment of why we’re a part of this community,” O’Gleby says, nearly choking up. “Everyone in the room—stage managers, costume, I mean everybody in the room—the way they were applauding these original cast members and what they gave to all of us as a community, really all over the world, it was incredible.”.

At the second rehearsal, on Monday night outside on 34th Street beneath Macy’s giant turkey, the mood remained high even as the temperatures dropped. By 11 p.m., performers were bundled in winter jackets, sweatshirts, and leg warmers, with their character shoes still on. They hugged one another for warmth and jumped up and down, kicking their feet to stay loose between setups. Margaret Cho, who stars as the Narrator in The Rocky Horror Show, danced “The Time Warp” with her Chihuahua, Lucia, tucked into a pouch in her jacket, the dog’s head peeking out.

Industry observers note that for O’Gleby, a smooth Monday-night rehearsal means setting each show up for success come Saturday morning and making sure all nine shows are “represented in the most powerful and clear storytelling way that we can,” she says. “This is a huge moment for these shows to sell lots of tickets so everyone gets to keep making their magic every night. And so it’s notable to me that each team gets to communicate what they need and what they think would really make their show shine.”.

On Wednesday afternoon, Macy's announced that “after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” a disappointing piece of news for those who build their holiday around the annual event.

In a recent development, this is only the fourth time in history that the parade hasn't been held on Thanksgiving: In 1942, 1943, and 1944 it was canceled completely as its trademark giant balloons were repurposed as part of the World War II effort. Compared to those years, a move to Saturday seems manageable, O’Gleby claims. “The weather will be what it will be, but we will delight in that and deliver the best.".

  • According to recent reports, then head to the Alexa mobile app and go to More in the top left (the three horizontal lines) > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping and toggle on Deal Recommendations under the Shopping Recommendations options.
  • It has been revealed that if Alexa finds an upcoming deal on something in your Saved for Later, your Wish List, or in your Shopping Cart, you’ll receive a pop-up alert on your Echo Show display or see a yellow light ring on your Echo speaker.

According to recent reports, amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale has officially started—but keeping track of the best discounts yet to land and figuring out which deals are worthwhile can be a challenge. As an alternative, you can have Alexa give you a heads-up about deals on products you already know you want to purchase, so you don’t have to spend time sorting through the noise.

According to recent reports, then head to the Alexa mobile app and go to More in the top left (the three horizontal lines) > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping and toggle on Deal Recommendations under the Shopping Recommendations options. This ensures you’ll receive notifications for items that appear in your shopping activity.

It has been revealed that if Alexa finds an upcoming deal on something in your Saved for Later, your Wish List, or in your Shopping Cart, you’ll receive a pop-up alert on your Echo Show display or see a yellow light ring on your Echo speaker. You can also ask, “Alexa, what are my notifications?” to hear a list of deals it has compiled thus far. You can also say "Alexa, let me know when [product name] goes on sale.".

Alexa can detect deals up to 24 hours in advance, so you can either ask it to remind you again when a deal starts or request that it buy the item when the deal goes live. Simply say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” and it’ll charge the default payment and send the item to the default delivery address on your account.

Industry observers note that marvel Rivals, the Overwatch-like hero shooter from NetEase and Marvel Games, is just a couple of weeks away from its second anniversary. To celebrate, The Lego Group is releasing a upcoming set based on the game's take on an iconic Marvel character. This will be the first-ever Marvel Rivals set, though plenty of Marvel sets already exist, and to mark the occasion, it will turn the beloved Jeff the Land Shark into a brick-built figure.

Recent findings suggest that jeff the Land Shark debuted in Kelly Thompson's West Coast Avengers in 2018 and has since become a mascot for Marvel across comics and games since.This includes Marvel Rivals, where he is playable as a Strategist hero. The Jeff the Land Shark lego set will be released on Jan. 1, 2027 and will cost $49.99​​​​​​​. You can pre-order it now at the official Lego store.

In a press release (via GameSpot), Lego Marvel design lead Jesper C. Nielsen mentioned that, "Jeff brings together everything players love about a breakout gaming character: an unforgettable silhouette, a personality you understand instantly, and the ability to turn any match into a story.”​​​​​​" He continued that the Lego team "wanted​​​​​​​ this Lego model to capture both sides of him, from the lovable companion fans want beside their screen to the unpredictable strategist they meet in battle.".

The Jeff the Land Shark set will be a modest 495 pieces in total and is rated for ages 12 and up. The store page states that once fully built, Jeff's head, legs, tail, and fins are all movable, allowing Jeff to be posed in multiple stances​​​​​​​. You can also detach his tongue and close his mouth. The fin can be detached as well, so you can move it around on the ground as if it were about to pop up on an enemy​​​​​​​.

NetEase Games will celebrate the second anniversary of Marvel Rivals by bringing its year-long Path to Doomsday event to a close​​​​​​​. At the end of the year​​​​​​​ Marvel fans can catch Avengers: Doomsday in theaters on Dec. 18. However, you won't be able to see it on IMAX screens, since Dune: Part 3 has those locked down.​​​​​​​.

Blade Runner 2099 Revives A Major Element From Philip K. Dick's Original Novel

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that any fan of "Blade Runner" knows that the source material for the film, Philip K.
  • To be fair, "Blade Runner" retains a surprising amount of Dick's novel, with whole swathes of dialogue making it all the way from the author's page to the screen.
  • This idea didn't make it to "Blade Runner" in any shape or form, however it does appear (and largely intact, too) in this month's "Blade Runner 2099" sequel series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that any fan of "Blade Runner" knows that the source material for the film, Philip K. Dick's novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," didn't exactly make it to the big screen fully intact. As influential and unique as it is, Dick's work proved too unwieldy for filmmakers to adapt wholesale. Instead, Hollywood took Dick's themes and concepts and heavily rewrote his stories for the screen. That trend began with "Blade Runner," as original screenwriter Hampton Fancher took the neo-noir concept from Dick's trippy, weird 1968 novel of a human hunting down illegal androids and pretty much discarded the rest. The relationship between "Androids" and "Blade Runner" can be succinctly summed up by the fact that Fancher and director Ridley Scott didn't use Dick's title for the film, eventually going so far as to borrow the title from a completely different novel by William S. Burroughs.

To be fair, "Blade Runner" retains a surprising amount of Dick's novel, with whole swathes of dialogue making it all the way from the author's page to the screen. Yet numerous other plot elements and characters were either altered or omitted altogether. One element in "Androids" which is very notable to Dick's worldbuilding is the concept of Mercerism, a religion in which devotees share a looping, pre-programmed experience via a virtual reality machine called an empathy box.

This idea didn't make it to "Blade Runner" in any shape or form, however it does appear (and largely intact, too) in this month's "Blade Runner 2099" sequel series. The use of Mercerism in the Prime Video show is a great example of showrunner Silka Luisa and her writers knowing Dick and "Blade Runner" well. In fact, the inclusion of a missing element of Dick's novel in a "Blade Runner" sequel is a bit of a franchise tradition.

According to recent reports, in "Blade Runner 2099," it initially seems that Silka Luisa and company have included Mercerism as a little Easter egg, as a couple of animated billboards in Los Angeles advertise it. Yet this isn't a winking reference to Philip K. Dick's novel, but is instead foreshadowing. In Episode 6, entitled "Kill the Killers," Cora (Hunter Schafer) and Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) travel to a hideaway where Cora and her brother grew up. It turns out this hideaway is a defunct Mercer Monastery, a place where those who worship the man could come to and use an empathy box or interact with automated priest-like programs (shades of George Lucas' "THX 1138" there).

Industry observers note that mercerism, as detailed in Dick's "Androids," is a religion based around the idea of increasing empathy, since the future of the novel has become so dystopian and isolating that people need to be reminded to have empathy for others (sound familiar?). This is done through the empathy box, which allows owners to experience a moment from the life of Wilbur Mercer, apparently some kind of martyr. In the box, Mercer endlessly climbs up a hill while being pelted with rocks, and the "empathy" the user experiences is holding onto sensors which deliver increasingly harsher shocks, sometimes resulting in death.

Industry observers note that the idea was first introduced by Dick in a short story in 1964 entitled "The Little Black Box," and then re-used in "Androids." The ironic twist in "Androids" is that Mercerism is revealed to be a total sham, with the video loop having been shot on a soundstage with an actor. Though this isn't addressed in "2099," the obvious decline in Mercerites and decay of the monastery implies that the religion isn't as popular as it once was.

Recent findings suggest that even though Mercerism didn't make it into a previous iteration of "Blade Runner," the themes behind it are so integral to the story of "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" and its world that its inclusion feels natural. "Blade Runner 2099" smoothly weaves it into its storyline, using it as an allegory for its doomed principal characters as well as its apocalyptic vision of Earth in general. It's used in the show in much the same way Dick uses it in "Androids," as a satiric commentary on how what was initially intended as an aspirational endeavor has devolved into something more pathetic than never believing in it in the first place.

Ironically, Mercerism is not the first element in "Androids" that was left out of "Blade Runner" but made a return appearance in a sequel story to Ridley Scott's film. In "Androids," the character of John R. Isidore (or J.R. Isidore) was reconceived and rewritten as J.F. Sebastian for "Blade Runner," and he was killed during the events of the film. However, when Dick's friend K.W. Jeter wrote the 1995 novel "Blade Runner 2: The Edge of Human," Jeter brought J.R. Isidore back into the story. It's not entirely clear if Jeter intends his Isidore to be the literal same character, or if he's "borrowing" the character in the same manner as Dick borrowed Mercerism from his short story for "Androids." Either way, it established a neat little tradition for the franchise, in which anything or anyone could come back, and perhaps come back different. For a series infamous for characters not ever fully knowing their true identity and heritage, the tradition feels rather poignant.

"Blade Runner 2099" is now streaming on Prime Video.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Avatar" fans can thank Eywa, because more sequels are indeed coming.
  • It has been revealed that was the future of a billion dollar franchise like "Avatar" ever in doubt?
  • According to recent reports, there's also the fact that director James Cameron, who has spent decades immersed in the world of Pandora, wants to direct other projects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Avatar" fans can thank Eywa, because more sequels are indeed coming. As reported by Collider, Disney's upcoming film release slate includes "Avatar 4" (dated for December 21, 2029) and "Avatar 5" (dated for December 19, 2031). These dates aren't necessarily etched in stone; during the 2010s, the release date for "Avatar: The Way of Water" got pushed back so much that many convinced themselves the movie was never coming out. You simply can't rush the quality that director James Cameron demands of the "Avatar" films. But it's a sign Disney wants the movies out sooner than later.

It has been revealed that was the future of a billion dollar franchise like "Avatar" ever in doubt? Keep in mind, the third movie, 2025's "Avatar: Fire and Ash," was the lowest grossing movie in the series. It still grossed just under $1.5 billion, but that's a notably diminished return next to "The Way of Water," which pulled $2.3 billion internationally. "Fire and Ash" was also, like its predecessors, one of the most expensive movies ever made.

According to recent reports, there's also the fact that director James Cameron, who has spent decades immersed in the world of Pandora, wants to direct other projects. Cameron is presently working on "Ghosts of Hiroshima," based on the non-fiction book by author Charles Pellegrino, and he's likewise attached to an adaptation of Joe Abercrombie's dark fantasy book "The Devils.".

Recent findings suggest that cameron, who is 72 years old, is in the stage of his life where he has to balance the films he wants to make against the time he has left, and he knows it. As he told the Empire Film podcast back in May 2026, he wants to make the fourth and fifth "Avatar" films in less time, and for less money, than it took to make "The Way of Water" and "Fire and Ash.".

Sources indicate that james Cameron told People in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will feature a six-year time jump. Parts of the film were even shot concurrently with "Fire and Ash" to capture the series' younger actors, like Jack Champion (Spider) and Trinity Bliss (Tuktirey), while they still pass as kids.

Industry observers note that the "Avatar" films have strong environmentalist themes; humanity wants to colonize Pandora because, by the 22nd century, Earth is polluted, overpopulated, and seemingly dying. We've only seen small glimpses of that in the previous films. Producer Jon Landau told Syfy back in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will change that:.

In a recent development, "There's over-population and a depletion of our natural resources that make life harder. But we don't want to paint a bleak picture for where our world is going. The films are also about the idea of that we can change course.".

What about lingering threads on Pandora? "Fire and Ash" ended with the recombinant Colonel Miles Quaritch (Stephen Lang) seemingly plummeting to his death. But one of the most essential rules of fiction is if you don't see a dead body, and sometimes even if you do, don't treat mortal peril as confirmed death.

It has been revealed that quaritch already beat death once, and it feels like he still hasn't quite completed his story yet. Even if Lang/Quaritch does sit "Avatar 4" out, "Fire and Ash" ended with his accomplice Varang (Oona Chaplin) still at large. Varang was easily the breakout character of "Fire and Ash," and I'd be shocked if we don't see her return to attack the Sully family again in movie number four.

"Avatar 4" is at the moment scheduled for theatrical release on December 21, 2029.

It has been revealed that what does “Michael Caine” sound like in the freezing cold? We’re about to find out with the just-announced release of “The Trip to the Northern Lights,” which is the reunion of Steve Coogan, Rob Brydon, and director Michael Winterbottom for what is the fifth installment of “The Trip” franchise of miniseries/movies.

According to recent reports, independent Film Firm and Sapan Studio picked up the U.S. rights to the fifth “Trip” film (IFC has released all four of the other films into theaters in the U.S.) and will release it theatrically on April 9, 2027. It will have been nearly seven years since the release of the last feature, and it sees Brydon now at 60 and Coogan at 59, so we’re guessing their ages may have made their wit and appetites even more ornery since. Related Stories ‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game.

“The Trip” movies are known for their food and travel porn as much as they are for their litany of impressions between Coogan and Brydon playing versions of themselves, but this one turns that concept on its head slightly by sending Coogan and Brydon up north, this time throughout Scandinavia, including Sweden and some islands in Norway, all in search of some other fine food and wry conversation.

The first look at the movie above sees the duo in ridiculously huge parkas in the snow as guided by some sled huskies. Try doing your best Bane impression at 10 below zero.

“We are very happy to be back on the road with IFC. They have been brilliant partners ever since the first ‘Trip’ all those years ago. ‘The Trip to the Northern Lights‘ takes Steve and Rob from Malmo in southern Sweden through Norway’s spectacular fjords to the Lofoten Islands in Norway’s Arctic circle,” Winterbottom remarked. “I hope the audience enjoys the journey as much as we did.”.

“The Trip” franchise began all the way back in 2011, and since then the films have spanned trips in England, Italy, Spain, and Greece. As has been the case with all of the installments, they’ve been miniseries airing on TV in England but then edited into films for the U.S. release. The first movie made $3.9 million worldwide across several re-releases, “The Trip to Italy” in 2014 made $6.1 million, 2017’s “The Trip to Spain” made $1.9 million, and “The Trip to Greece” in the COVID-addled summer 2020 still managed to make $259K worldwide.

All four of the “Trip” movies are at the moment available for streaming on Sun Now, which is the streamer owned by Independent Film Organization parent AMC Global Media.

It has been revealed that “The Independent Film Tech giant is thrilled to continue our longstanding relationship with this world-class group of filmmakers on the latest installment of this beloved franchise. Few comedic partnerships have the enduring appeal of Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon, and under Michael Winterbottom’s inspired direction, each fresh trip remains the comedic gift that keeps on giving. This time around, we can’t wait for audiences to join us on the road to the Northern Lights,” mentioned Ayo Kepher-Maat, Independent Film Company’s Vice President of Acquisitions and Production.

In a recent development, “Michael Winterbottom, Steve Coogan, and Rob Brydon have created a franchise filled with taste, wit and belly laughs. Independent Film Company has brought each one to audiences with characteristic care and capability. ‘The Trip to the Northern Lights’ advances the history with the delight of something completely fresh and tasty,” said Josh Sapan of Sapan Studio.

It has been revealed that the film is produced by Melissa Parmenter and Josh Hyams for Revolution Films. The deal was negotiated by Ayo Kepher-Maat on behalf of Independent Film Organization and Tristan Whalley MD of Goalpost Films on behalf of the filmmakers.

Executive producers are Winterbottom, Coogan, Brydon, Alex Moody, Josh Sapan, Tristan Whalley, Paul Wiegard. “The Trip to the Northern Lights” is a Revolution Films, Baby Cow, and Small Man Production in association with Sky Studios.

Deadline first reported the news of the acquisition.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. The price you pay for Amazon depends on many factors, but regardless of how much you're paying, it's worth it for most people (we've done the math).

According to recent reports, if you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the organization is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

Industry observers note that the standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

Industry observers note that I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):.

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

Amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

It has been revealed that sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

Sources indicate that amazon Health: Prime people get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance prepares, too.

Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.

Avengers: Secret Wars Setting Confirmed By Marvel, Spoiling Doomsday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It looks like we're heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe's version of Battleworld in "Avengers: Secret Wars." The final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer promises a major showdown between Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor von Doom and a conglomerate of heroes from various timelines.
  • We've known for some time that one of Marvel Comics' greatest modern writers, Jonathan Hickman, is a secret MCU consultant, and that "Avengers: Doomsday" is loosely adapting his "Avengers: Time Runs Out" storyline from 2014.
  • Sources indicate that the Marvel Studios president told the outlet, "'Secret Wars' is different than any other movie we've ever made.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It looks like we're heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe's version of Battleworld in "Avengers: Secret Wars." The final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer promises a major showdown between Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor von Doom and a conglomerate of heroes from various timelines. As it stands, "Doomsday" has a real shot at the biggest box office opening weekend ever, which would bode very well for the second part of Joe and Anthony Russo's upcoming duology, "Avengers: Secret Wars." That sequel is due out on December 17, 2027, and if "Doomsday" does what "Infinity War" did back in 2018, it should have a grand old time at the box office. That is, if Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige doesn't spoil things before then.

We've known for some time that one of Marvel Comics' greatest modern writers, Jonathan Hickman, is a secret MCU consultant, and that "Avengers: Doomsday" is loosely adapting his "Avengers: Time Runs Out" storyline from 2014. That arc serves as a prelude to Hickman's 2015 "Secret Wars" storyline, and together these two runs see the Marvel universe collapse due to "incursions," after which Victor von Doom uses fragments of the shattered multiverse to create a upcoming planet named Battleworld. In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, Feige basically confirmed that this is the setting for the MCU's version of "Secret Wars," basically spoiling "Doomsday" by strongly hinting how that film ends and where the next one begins.

Sources indicate that the Marvel Studios president told the outlet, "'Secret Wars' is different than any other movie we've ever made. Look at the comics. The characters and the settings and the worlds within this singular planet where our movie 'Secret Wars' takes place is the imagination gone wild, which is what's exciting about it." So there you have it. Most fans expected to see Battleworld in "Secret Wars," but now it's as close to official as you can get.

The first "Secret Wars" comic book arc arrived in 1984, with writer Jim Shooter and artists Mike Zeck and Bob Layton delivering a story in which the cosmic entity known as The Beyonder forced various Marvel characters to fight to the death on the planet Battleworld. It seems Marvel Studios will draw from this original run for some aspects of "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Avengers: Secret Wars." But for the most part, Jonathan Hickman's 2015 run serves as the basis for the two movies.

In a recent development, this second "Secret Wars" arc, illustrated by artist Esad Ribić with cover designs by Alex Ross, and the run that preceded it, "Time Runs Out," are the essential inspiration for "Doomsday" and its sequel. Feige told Entertainment Weekly that "Doomsday" is basically the MCU's version of "Time Runs Out," while the filmmakers described "Secret Wars" as "a little bit of both" that storyline and Hickman's "Secret Wars.".

Asked to comment further, Feige said, "If you wanted spoilers for 'The Odyssey,' you could go read the book. If you want spoilers for 'Doomsday' and 'Secret Wars,' you can go look at the comics," adding, "It is very much the same thing that we're doing." Clearly, then, Hickman's work is integral to the two upcoming MCU releases, with Feige going on to say that "Secret Wars" is "very much" the "culmination of an incursion, multiversal-collapse event." With that in mind, you can bet the "Doomsday" sequel will play out pretty much entirely on the MCU's version of Battleworld, with the surviving heroes from "Doomsday" taking the fight to its god emperor, Doom, in an attempt to overthrow his regime and restore the multiverse. Whether "Secret Wars" will include Marvel's infamous Spider-Man bathroom scene, however, remains unconfirmed.

None of Kevin Feige's latest revelations should come as a big shock to Marvel fans who've known Marvel Studios has been drawing from Jonathan Hickman's "Secret Wars" run. But this is the closest Feige has come to officially confirming Battleworld as the setting for "Avengers: Secret Wars." The Marvel Studios head didn't use the name "Battleworld," but his comments about a "singular planet" were in response to a question about it.

Otherwise, Feige characterized "Avengers: Doomsday" as "a culmination of what's come before," and "Secret Wars" as "a launching pad for [Marvel Studios'] films in 2028 — the 20th anniversary of the MCU." Clearly, then, whatever happens at the end of "Secret Wars" will set the stage for fresh characters, timelines, and storylines that will reshape the way the MCU looks going forward.

According to recent reports, we know that Marvel Studios is preparing its Jake Schrier-directed X-Men movie, which is set to debut in the wake of "Secret Wars." First, though, Marvel is reworking its cinematic universe with "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars." According to co-director Joe Russo, this simply had to be done with two movies due to it being "such a major storyline." He continued: "Doom as a character needs a lot of space, especially when Robert Downey is playing him. So the scale of the story, the emotional scale of the story is so large that it really needed to be a two-parter.".

Industry observers note that whether the second part of that two-parter will actually debut on December 17, 2027, however, remains unclear. Production on "Secret Wars" has been moved to 2027, suggesting a delay might be imminent. For now, we'll have to wait and see how things play out. But regardless of when the movie actually arrives, prepare yourselves for a massive screen visit to Battleworld.

Industry observers note that “Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo,” a Japan-set take on police decadence, will open in North America on March 5, 2027. Neon, the Oscar-winning studio behind “Anora” and “Parasite,” is distributing the film.

Directed by Takashi Miike, the Japanese auteur behind “Audition” and “13 Assassins,” “”Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo” stars Shun Oguri (“Godzilla v. Kong”), Lily James (“Pam and Tommy”), and WWE star Liv Morgan. It follows a veteran police detective Yabuki (Oguri), who is struggling with drug addiction, gambling debts, and guilt over past misdeeds, as he chases a shadowy killer tied to organized crime through Tokyo. His case ends up intersecting with that of an American FBI agent (James), who’s hunting a missing tourist (Morgan). Related Stories ‘The Trip’ Returns for Fifth Installment, Next Sending Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon to Frigid Arctic Circle ‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain.

Industry observers note that the film had its world premiere at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival, where it earned mixed notices, with some reviewers faulting it as overstuffed. Neon is in the midst of a busy fall, with the indie studio releasing awards contenders such as “All of a Sudden,” “Fjord,” “Paper Tiger,” and “Artificial,” so it makes sense that it would opt to have “Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo” come out in the spring.

“Bad Lieutenant” first entered the cinematic vernacular with Abel Ferrara’s 1992 crime thriller that was so boundary-pushing (a nun is raped) it received an NC-17 rating. It also offered up Harvey Keitel at his most unhinged and committed, playing a cop who broke really, really bad. Then Werner Herzog transported the depravity to the Big Easy with 2009’s “Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call Newly introduced Orleans,” featuring Nicolas Cage at his most gonzo. Thus, an unlikely franchise was born.

The latest “Bad Lieutenant” is a U.S.-Japan co-production, produced by the late Jeremy Thomas for Recorded Picture Tech giant, Sam Pressman for Pressman Film, Naoaki Kitajima for Nippon TV, and Misako Saka for OLM.
